https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/.text: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) – A Russian ballistic missile and drone barrage across Ukraine overnight killed at least eight civilians, including children, and injured more than 50 others, officials said Thursday, and NATO scrambled its warplanes after one of the missiles crossed the country’s western border into Poland. The blitz expanded Russia´s almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities, including the capital of Kyiv where tens of thousands spent the night sheltering in subway stations, as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv´s critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defenses. NATO said a Russian missile entered Polish airspace during the onslaught and landed in a rural area. It caused no injuries or damage but could deepen tensions between the military alliance and Moscow, as wary European countries fear the 4-year-old war could spill into their territory. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called it “yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine.” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it was “a very serious incident,” but added: “There are absolutely no reasons to believe that Poland was the target.” Russia’s barrage struck areas of Ukraine where weapons are believed to be stored and manufactured. Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia’s oil sector, causing a fuel crisis. The attack came two days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with U.S. President Donald Trump and representatives of American defense companies as he pleads for swifter and bigger deliveries of Patriot air defense systems to stop Russia´s ballistic missiles. The Iran war has drained stockpiles of the U.S.-made interceptors. Trump has promised to grant Ukraine licenses to build its own Patriots, but production could take many months. “Given the critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism,” Zelenskyy said on social media. “This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people,” he said. Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged. Russia launched more than 70 missiles, a significant number of them ballistic missiles, he said, and over 280 attack drones, of which more than 260 were intercepted. The Russian Defense Ministry said it targeted Ukrainian air bases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities, including drone factories and storage depots, as well as plants for missiles, aircraft repairs, electronics and chemicals. In the Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russian attack killed six people and wounded 10, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, in a post on Telegram. Children were among the dead – a 6-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17 in the area of Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, Hanzha added. The children´s parents were killed in the same attack, but two more children were pulled alive from the rubble, Zelenskyy said. “It was an ordinary home, blown (to) smithereens by a ballistic missile,” he said on X. In Kyiv, Russian forces struck the capital with ballistic missiles, killing a 31-year-old man and wounding two others, the National Police press service said. More than 56,000 people sheltered in Kyiv´s subway stations overnight, according to the Facebook post from the metro system. A cruise missile attack struck the western city of Lviv, killing one person and wounding over 30, including children aged 6, 13 and 15, said Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv regional military administration. In the Poltava region, a drone hit warehouses, killing one person, said regional military head Vitalii Diakivnych. Russian forces also dropped three powerful glide bombs on an industrial zone in the southern city of Kherson, killing a 56-year-old man, local officials said. A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland overnight, violating NATO airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X, calling it a clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine´s air defenses would also guarantee wider European security. Responding to the missile alert, NATO forces in Poland scrambled two fighter jets, an attack helicopter and two other aircraft, and activated ground defenses, said Col. Michael O´Connell, the spokesperson for the alliance´s military command in Belgium. The missile quickly disappeared from radar, the Polish Armed Forces said. A helicopter flew to its last known location, where the crew discovered a probable impact site in a farming area in Lublin province, the command said. Investigators found fragments indicating that the object was a Kh-101 missile, Polish news agency PAP reported. Tusk had met with Zelenskyy in Lublin on Wednesday to discuss defense issues. NATO military commander Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich told Poland´s Defense Chief Gen. Wieslaw Kukulan the military alliance “will continue to take all necessary measures to defend NATO territory,” O´Donnell said. Meanwhile, Russia´s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight. A depot belonging to Wildberries online retailer was set ablaze in Russia’s Penza region southeast of Moscow, in the latest strike on the company’s warehouses, Penza Gov. Oleg Melnichenko. Four people were injured and 200 workers were evacuated, he said, adding that about 100 firefighters were deployed. Wildberries also reported its warehouse in Sarapul in the Udmurtia region more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) from Ukraine, was struck by a Ukrainian drone and set ablaze. It said the workers had been safely evacuated. The Russian online news outlet Astra reported that another Wildberries depot in the Perm region in the Urals was also set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone strike. Regional authorities reported a Ukrainian drone attack but didn´t give information about the damage. Thursday´s attacks on Wildberries warehouses brought to 14 the number of the retailer´s depots struck by Ukrainian drones in under two weeks. Ukraine accuses Wildberries of supplying goods that can be used by the Russian military. Ukrainian drone units destroyed four more vessels belonging to Russia´s “shadow fleet” of sanctions-busting tankers, bringing the total to 205 since the operation began July 6, Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on his Telegram channel. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Helen Haines Car allegedly did U-turn and struck Helen Haines twice, in what some believe was targeted attack against MP Independent MP is in critical yet stable condition, as police interview alleged attacker in Wangaratta incident Follow our Helen Haines live blog for latest updates Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria? Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Tess Ikonomou and Tom McIlroy Mon 19 Oct 2026 21.50 EDT First published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in what some believed may be a targeted attack near her electorate office, according to eyewitnesses. The independent MP remains in a critical condition after being airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night. A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota Land Cruiser was arrested at the scene. The alleged attacker has been named as Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent , Guardian Australia has confirmed. Helen Haines: independent MP in critical condition in Melbourne’s Alfred hospital after being struck by car in Wangaratta – follow updates Read more Police were expected to interview the suspect in the attack on Tuesday, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said. The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said witnesses alleged the driver completed a U-turn before the incident. “What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time,” he told ABC radio. “A bystander ran towards the scene, got the driver out of the vehicle and held the driver until police arrived.” Ricky Jefferies, whose barbershop is next door to Haines’ office, ran from his shop to help after hearing the crash. “I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,” he told reporters on Tuesday morning. View image in fullscreen Barber Ricky Jefferies speaks to media outside his Wangaratta barbershop, next door to Helen Haines’ constituency office. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images Jefferies, who returned to work on Tuesday morning, alleged the driver had a knife on him. “He didn’t pull it out,” he said. “Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away.” Burke said: “I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place.” The home affairs minister said the nation’s security agencies and police will be working through what more could have been done to prevent the alleged attack and to help keep others safe. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email On Monday Burke reported that there had been 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, an increase from 951 the year before. “We we already knew that we needed to do more to be able to keep people in public office safe and we have been,” he said. “While we don’t make public the dollar figures and the and the exact provision of security for obvious reasons … we had a very significant uplift in the budget. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action.” View image in fullscreen A woman places flowers outside the office of federal independent MP Helen Haines in the Victorian regional city of Wangaratta. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has been joined by leaders and parliamentarians from across the country in calling for a calming of political discourse. Helen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her life Read more The mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, expressed gratitude to Jeffries for stepping in to stop the man. “I spoke to the barber this morning and he just shrugged his shoulders. He seemed to just take it in his stride. This was something that he had to do and he did it,” she said. “He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.” View image in fullscreen Haines was airlifted to Alfred hospital in Melbourne for treatment for critical injuries. Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty Images Wangaratta, the rural city in which the incident occurred, is a tight-knit community in north-east Victoria. At the last census it had a population of about 20,000 people, while the broader LGA had just under 30,000. Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been key to the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission, as well as campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access and pushing back on misuse of taxpayer funds, or pork barrelling. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: People protest on the street near Congress, following former President Santiago Pena's removal from office in an impeachment trial that looked at his connections to digital lender Ueno. Photograph: César Olmedo/Reuters View image in fullscreen People protest on the street near Congress, following former President Santiago Pena's removal from office in an impeachment trial that looked at his connections to digital lender Ueno. Photograph: César Olmedo/Reuters Paraguay Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts Santiago Peña was detained minutes after he was impeached by Congress, as protesters took to the streets demanding answers after the suspension of the Ueno bank Tiago Rogero South America correspondent Fri 6 Nov 2026 20.55 EST Last modified on Fri 6 Nov 2026 20.56 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Paraguay’s rightwing president has been placed under house arrest minutes after he was impeached by Congress, amid a severe crisis that left more than half the country’s population unable to access their bank accounts. Santiago Peña is being investigated about allegations he used his political influence to favour a bank that expanded exponentially under his government and was suspended this week after irregularities . The move froze the accounts of 2.9 million people, about 60% of the country’s adult population, who were customers of the bank – Ueno - and who overnight could no longer use their own money even for basic purchases such as bread and water. Protests spread across the country, some involving violent clashes with police. Impeachment proceedings began on Wednesday before being concluded on Friday, minutes before Peña’s arrest was ordered. His vice-president, Pedro Alliana, was being sworn in as the country’s new leader while a public prosecutor, accompanied by police outside Peña’s home, told local media the former president had been placed under house arrest. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators take part in a protest against the banking crisis. Photograph: Jose Bogado/AFP/Getty Images “It has been established that he is indeed inside his home. He voluntarily allowed officers to enter and made himself available for all procedural purposes,” said prosecutor Elena Fiore Franco. The public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into Peña on Thursday on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling. Peña, who was one of US president Donald Trump’s main allies in the region, had tried to resign on Thursday in an attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who become senators for life in Paraguay – but lawmakers did not accept his resignation, leaving him subject to the ordinary courts. Amid rumours he had fled to Argentina, the 47-year-old economist was expected to appear before Congress to present his defence during the impeachment proceedings, but left that to his lawyers and instead continued posting on social media. View image in fullscreen A file photo of Paraguay’s impeached president Santiago Peña. Photograph: César Olmedo/Reuters Before the impeachment was concluded or the arrest warrant issued, he posted: “I say goodbye with gratitude, while fully recognising the anguish of those who are now waiting for answers,” referring to former Ueno customers who are unable to access their own money. Soon after taking office, Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, a former CEO of Ueno, head of the country’s central bank. Three months later, Spalding – who was by now regulating the company he used to run – allowed Ueno to become a digital bank, which put it on the path to becoming one of Paraguay’s largest banks by deposits in just a few years. The arrest warrant for Peña also includes Spalding. Peña himself had about US$1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”. View image in fullscreen Pedro Alliana is sworn in as president of Paraguay on Friday. Photograph: Nathalia Aguilar/Anadolu/Getty Images As the bank aggressively expanded through an easy account-opening system and by promising returns far above those offered by the rest of the market, it also managed to bring public pension funds controlled by Peña’s administration into its portfolio. “Because Ueno had the blessing of the presidency, most of the pension funds close to the government went to deposit their money in the bank,” said political analyst Hugo Duarte. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno. As pressure mounted and retail sales fell by as much as 80% because much of the population could not access their own money, Peña lost the support of his own party. During the impeachment session, opposition senator Rafael Filizzola said Paraguay was facing “one of the biggest corruption scandals since the return of democracy” and the “biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era”.
